paragraphs.heading: Mixing orbitals
paragraphs.text: Orbital hybridisation is the idea that an atom can blend its atomic orbitals into a new set of hybrid orbitals. An orbital is a model of how electrons behave inside molecules. The new hybrids differ from the originals in energy and shape, and they are suited to pairing up electrons into chemical bonds. The idea belongs to valence bond theory, and it looks at bonding from the point of view of one atom. Usually the orbitals that get mixed have similar energies.

paragraphs.heading: The puzzle of methane
paragraphs.text: Linus Pauling put forward the theory in 1931 to explain the shapes of simple molecules such as methane, CH₄. Here was the puzzle. Carbon makes its four bonds using one s orbital and three p orbitals, so you might expect three bonds at right angles plus a fourth, weaker bond pointing in some arbitrary direction. Real methane looks nothing like that. Its four C–H bonds are equally strong, and any two of them meet at about 109.5°.

paragraphs.heading: Pauling's answer
paragraphs.text: Pauling proposed that, with four hydrogen atoms nearby, carbon combines its s and p orbitals into four equal mixtures, which he named hybrid orbitals. Each one is labelled sp³ to show its recipe, and each points along one of the four C–H bonds. In methane each hybrid has 25% s character and 75% p character. To get four half-filled orbitals, carbon first promotes an electron from its 2s orbital into an empty 2p orbital. That costs energy, but forming two extra bonds releases more than enough to make up for it.

paragraphs.heading: Double bonds and sp²
paragraphs.text: Other molecules can be explained the same way. Ethylene, C₂H₄, has a double bond between its two carbons. Here each carbon mixes its 2s orbital with only two of its three 2p orbitals, giving three sp² hybrids and leaving one p orbital unmixed. One sp² orbital from each carbon overlaps to make a σ (sigma) bond, and the leftover p orbitals overlap to make a π (pi) bond that sits perpendicular to the plane of the molecule. Each carbon also bonds to two hydrogens, with all bond angles at 120°.

paragraphs.heading: Why chemists still use it
paragraphs.text: The idea began with simple molecules but was later applied much more widely. Today it counts as an effective rule of thumb for working out the structures of organic compounds, and it gives a simple orbital picture that matches Lewis structures. It explains the bonding in methane and in alkenes. How much s or p character an atom's orbitals carry, which hybridisation mostly decides, can even be used to predict properties such as acidity or basicity.

paragraphs.heading: A telling example
paragraphs.text: Methylene, CH₂, shows why some mixing is needed. If carbon used only its two half-filled p orbitals to bond the two hydrogens, the H–C–H angle would be 90°, the angle between two p orbitals on one atom. In singlet methylene the real angle is about 102°. That gap points to some orbital hybridisation taking place.
